## merge vs rebase

**merge** — join two branches, keep full history. Creates merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
     \
      D---E  feature
           \
            M  ← merge commit (has 2 parents)
```

**rebase** — replay feature commits on top of target. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
             \
              D'--E'  ← replayed commits (new hashes)
```

---

## when use each

**merge when:**
- shared/public branch (never rewrite pushed commits)
- want preserve exact history + context
- merging into `main`/`master`
- team needs audit trail

**rebase when:**
- local feature branch, not yet pushed
- want clean linear history before PR
- updating feature branch with latest main changes
- squashing messy WIP commits

---

## tradeoffs

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| history | true, messy | clean, rewritten |
| conflicts | once | per replayed commit |
| safe on public branch | ✅ | ❌ |
| bisect/log readability | harder | easier |
| preserves timestamps | ✅ | ❌ |

---

## golden rule

> Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branch.

Rebase rewrites hashes. Others have old hashes. Chaos follow.

---

## common pattern

```bash
# update feature branch cleanly
git checkout feature
git rebase main        # replay feature on top of main

# then merge to main (fast-forward, no merge commit)
git checkout main
git merge feature
```

Result: linear history, no noise.
